L155: the fourth quarter of 2000 the Company merged with Security Systems  Integration
L156: (SSI)  through  an  exchange  of stock.  This  transaction  added a very  strong
L157: Government  Division to the Company.  In addition to its headquarters  office in
L158: Springfield,  Virginia, which is in the Washington,  D.C. metropolitan area, the
L159: Company has regional offices in Atlanta and Dallas and Sacramento, California.
L160: Integrated Security Systems
L161:          Integrated security systems are comprised of one or more subsystems and
L162: components that perform a variety of security  functions for a facility or group
L163: of facilities under the direction of a single command center. The command center
L164: consists of a central  processor,  a common  database and  software  that enable
L165: various  subsystems and components to communicate  with each other and integrate
L166: the subsystems and  components  into a single system.  Subsystems and components
L167: consist primarily of the following:
L168:          Access  control  systems,  which are  designed to exclude  unauthorized
L169: personnel  from  specified  areas and provide  access  control that is typically
L170: card-activated.  Entry and exit activity can be monitored or recorded and may be
L171: controlled on the basis of time and authority level.
L172:          Intrusion detection systems,  which incorporate  ultrasonic,  infrared,
L173: microwave and other  sensors to detect  unauthorized  door and window  openings,
L174: glass breakage,  vibration,  motion and noise,  and alarms and other  peripheral
L175: equipment.
L176:          Closed circuit television  systems,  which monitor and record entry and
L177: exit activity or provide  surveillance  of designated  areas.  These systems can
L178: deter theft and vandalism and support other access control systems.  They can be
L179: monitored either by a video recorder or by a monitoring screen.
L180:          Critical condition  monitoring  systems,  which provide  supervision of
L181: various   systems  and  processes  such  as  sprinkler   systems,   heating  and
L182: refrigeration  systems,  power  levels,  water levels and general  manufacturing
L183: processes.
L184: 
L185:          Fire detection systems, which incorporate heat,  ionization,  smoke and
L186: flame sensing devices,  manual pull stations,  evacuation  sounders and systems,
L187: sprinkler systems and elevator controls.
L188: 
L189: The Company's Services
L190:          The Company  offers a full range of security  services,  consisting of:
L191: (i)  consulting  and  planning;  (ii)  engineering  and  design;  (iii)  systems
L192: integration;  and (iv)  maintenance and technical  support.  At the beginning of
L193: each new client  relationship,  the Company  designates one of its  professional
L194: staff as the client  service  contact.  This  individual  is the focal point for
L195: communications between the Company and the client and often acts as the client's
L196: project  manager for all of its security  needs.  The Company's  engagement  may
L197: include one or more of the elements described below.
L198:          Consulting  and  Planning.  Security  consulting  and  planning are the
L199: initial phases of determining a security solution for a project. The Company has
L200: developed  a  planning  process  that  identifies  all  systems,   policies  and
L201: procedures  that are required for the successful  operation of a security system
L202: that will both meet a  client's  current  needs and  accommodate  its  projected
L203: future requirements.  The Company's consulting and planning process includes the
L204: following steps:
L205: Identify the client's objectives and security system requirements
L206: 
L207: Review the existing security system plan
L208: 
L209: Survey the site,  including  inventory of physical  components  and software and
L210: evaluation of client's existing infrastructure and security system
L211: 
L212: Identify and prioritize the client's vulnerabilities
L213: 
L214: Develop and evaluate system alternatives
L215: 
L216: Recommend a conceptual security plan design
L217: 
L218: Estimate the cost of implementing the conceptual plan
L219: 
L220: Develop a preliminary implementation schedule
L221:          As a result of this  process,  the Company  provides  the client with a
L222: master  plan for  security  services  which  recommends  an  effective  security
L223: solution that addresses routine operating needs as well as emergency situations.
L224: The Company believes that its comprehensive planning process enables its clients
L225: to  budget  for their  security  requirements  on a  long-term  basis,  identify
L226: opportunities for cost reduction and prepare for future risks.
L227:          Engineering and Design.  The  engineering  and design process  involves
L228: preparation of detailed project specifications and working drawings by a team of
L229: the Company's  engineers,  systems  designers and  computer-aided  design system
L230: operators.  These specifications and drawings detail the instrument  sensitivity
L231: requirements,   layout  of  the  control  center,  placement  of  equipment  and
L232: electrical  requirements.  Throughout the engineering  and design  process,  the
L233: Company utilizes its expertise in advanced technologies and its understanding of
L234: its  client's  operational  preferences  to design a system that is  functional,
L235: cost-effective and accommodates the client's present and future requirements. In
L236: addition,  the Company attempts to incorporate its client's existing  personnel,
L237: equipment and other physical resources into the system design.
L238:          When  retained  as  a  single-source   provider  for  turnkey  security
L239: solutions,  the Company also selects the system  components  required  under the
L240: specifications and drawings it has prepared. To the extent possible, the Company
L241: uses  off-the-shelf   equipment  to  minimize  the  cost  of  developing  custom
L242: equipment.  The Company  has made a  strategic  decision  not to  represent  any
L243: equipment  manufacturer   exclusively,   thereby  maintaining   objectivity  and
L244: flexibility  in equipment  selection.  The Company  believes  that its technical
L245: proficiency  with the  products of a wide range of  manufacturers  enables it to
L246: select components that will best meet a project's requirements.
L247:          Systems   Integration.   Systems  integration  involves  (i)  equipment
L248: procurement;  (ii) custom  systems  modeling  and  fabrication;  (iii)  facility
L249: installation;  (iv) hardware,  software and network integration;  and (v) system
L250: validation and testing.  In addition to these basic  integration  services,  the
L251: Company  provides  engineering  services  to enhance  the  compatibility  of the
L252: client's subsystems.  The Company prepares technical documentation of the system
L253: and operations manuals and provides on-site training to client personnel.
L254:          Under the supervision of a project manager,  the Company's  technicians
L255: conduct  hardware  installation,   hardware  and  software  integration,  system
L256: validation and testing. The aspects of systems integration that do not require a
L257: high  level  of  technical  expertise,  such  as  wire  installation  and  basic
L258: construction, are typically performed by the Company's subcontractors.
L259:          Maintenance and Technical Support. The Company provides maintenance and
L260: technical support services on a scheduled,  on-call,  or emergency basis.  These
L261: services  include  developing  and  implementing  maintenance  programs both for
L262: security  systems  designed,  engineered,  or  integrated by the Company and for
L263: existing systems.
L264:          Maintenance services offered by the Company include its EMS, a database
L265: used by the  Company  to  effectively  manage a  security  system's  components,
L266: maintenance  planning  and  scheduling,  and  costs.  The  system  configuration
L267: function  monitors  system  activity and capacity,  and  identifies  the need to
L268: reconfigure or expand the system. The system maintenance  function schedules and
L269: records maintenance activity, and identifies equipment replacement and upgrading
L270: requirements.

L274: Marketing
L275:          The Company's  marketing  activities are conducted on both national and
L276: regional  levels.  The Company obtains  engagements  through  existing  contract
L277: vehicles with commercial and government  organizations,  direct negotiation with
L278: clients,  competitive bid processes and referrals.  At the national  level,  the
L279: Company  conducts  analyses of various  government  agencies and  industries and
L280: targets those with  significant  potential demand for security  solutions.  At a
L281: regional level, under the supervision of senior management, each office develops
L282: and implements a marketing plan for its region. The plan identifies  prospective
L283: clients within the region and sets forth a strategy for developing relationships
L284: with them. Each regional office works with the headquarters  office in expanding
L285: relationships  with existing  national,  commercial  and  government  clients to
L286: include facilities within the region.
L287:          The Company has  identified  several key  industries or facility  types
L288: that it believes  have  substantial  and  increasing  requirements  for security
L289: services,  including  telecommunication  and  technology  companies,   corporate
L290: complexes and industries and facilities for which security  systems are required
L291: by regulation.  The Company has developed expertise in the security  regulations
L292: applicable to airports, pharmaceutical companies, prisons and nuclear utilities,
L293: military  chemical  demilitarization   facilities,  U.S.  Military  installation
L294: facilities and classified government facilities.
L295:          The  Company's  marketing  strategy  emphasizes   developing  long-term
L296: relationships  with clients that have multiple  facilities and complex  security
L297: requirements  so that the  Company  can  continue  to  provide  services  over a
L298: recurring basis after the initial contract.  The Company undertakes  significant
L299: pre-assessment  of a  prospective  client's  needs before an initial  contact is
L300: made. A long-term  relationship  typically  begins with an engagement to provide
L301: consulting  and  planning  or  maintenance  and  technical   support   services.
L302: Consulting  and  planning  assignments  place  the  Company  in an  advantageous
L303: position,  often as the client's project manager, to be engaged to implement the
L304: plan ultimately adopted by the client. Engagements for maintenance and technical
L305: support  enable the Company to identify  new  requirements  as they arise and to
L306: offer its  solutions  to such  requirements.  In the  Government  Division,  the
L307: Company has developed strong relationships and open-ended contract vehicles that
L308: allow the Company to provide  recurring  services to its  customers  for several
L309: years.  AS a result of successful  performance,  the Company  receives  positive
L310: references  and  referrals  from  its  existing   customers  to  new  government
L311: customers.

L377: Competition
L378:          The security industry is highly competitive.  The Company competes on a
L379: local,  regional and national basis with systems  integrators,  consulting firms
L380: and  engineering  and design  firms.  The Company  believes  that it is the only
L381: provider that focuses solely on its comprehensive  range of security services to
L382: government and commercial  clients on a national basis. As a result, the Company
L383: competes with different  companies  depending upon the nature of the project and
L384: the services  being  offered.  For example,  the Company has competed  with ADT,
L385: Systems  Technology  Group (STG) and Mosler for systems  integration  work,  and
L386: Lockwood  Greene and Holmes & Narver for consulting and planning and engineering
L387: and design work.  Many of its  competitors  have greater  name  recognition  and
L388: financial  resources than the Company.  The Company may face future  competition
L389: from potential new entrants into the security industry and increased competition
L390: from existing  competitors  that may attempt to develop the ability to offer the
L391: full range of  services  offered  by the  Company.  The  Company  believes  that
L392: competition  is  based  primarily  on the  ability  to  deliver  solutions  that
L393: effectively meet a client's  requirements  and, to a lesser extent and primarily
L394: in  competitive  bid  situations,  on price.  There can be no assurance that the
L395: Company will be able to compete  successfully in the future against  existing or
L396: potential competitors.
L397: Backlog
L398:          The  Company's  backlog  consists of confirmed  orders,  including  the
L399: balance of projects in process. The backlog also includes projects for which the
L400: Company  has been  notified  it is the  successful  bidder even though a binding
L401: agreement has not been executed.  Projects for which a binding  contract has not
L402: been executed may be canceled at any time. Binding contracts may also be subject
L403: to cancellation or postponement,  although cancellation  generally obligates the
L404: client to pay the costs incurred by the Company. Long-term maintenance contracts
L405: may be canceled  without cause.  As of December 31, 1999 and 2000, the Company's
L406: backlog was approximately $6.7 million and $6.75 million, respectively.  Backlog
L407: as of December 31, 2000,  includes projects having a value of approximately $2.5
L408: million for which  binding  contracts  have not been executed and all backlog is
L409: expected to be completed  during 2001.  Backlog orders as of any particular date
L410: may not be indicative of actual operating  results for any fiscal period.  There
L411: can be no assurance that any amount of backlog will be realized.  In addition to
L412: backlog,  the  Company  has  potential  follow-on  projects  with  its  existing
L413: customers of another  $19.7  million.  These are projects  which the Company has
L414: been informed that are likely to happen over the next 12 to 24 months.
L415: Employees
L416:          As of December 31, 2000, the Company had 87 employees, of which 40 were
L417: based in the  Company's  headquarters  located  in  Springfield,  Virginia.  The
L418: balance work out of the company's  regional  offices.  Thirteen of the Company's
L419: employees  are engaged  exclusively  in  marketing  and sales,  60  employees in

L421: executive  management and  administration.  None of the Company's  employees are
L422: represented by a labor union and the Company believes its employee relations are

L472: Liquidity and Capital Resources
L473:          Through 1997, the Company funded its capital requirements with cash
L474: generated by operations, private equity offerings, and its initial public
L475: offering in October 1997. During April 1998, the Board of Directors approved the
L476: issuance of up to $2.0 million of convertible subordinated debentures to provide
L477: additional working capital. As of May 13, 1998, the Company had issued and sold
L478: $1,450,000 of debentures. The Company sold an additional $400,000 of debentures
L479: as of August 25, 1998. The debentures have an interest rate of 10%, are due on
L480: December 31, 1999 and are convertible into common stock of the Company at $8.50
L481: per share. In addition, the holders were issued 100 warrants for each $1,000 of
L482: investment with an exercise price of $2.50 and a term of three years.
L483:          During February 1999, the $1.9 million the Company was required to post
L484: as collateral for a bond pending its appeal of a law suit was released when the
L485: trial court's judgment was reversed. The Company paid off $0.9 million of the
L486: convertible subordinated debentures during the first quarter 1999. In September
L487: 1999 all of the holders of the remaining subordinated debentures agreed to
L488: exchange their notes for the Company's common stock valued at $1.50 per share.
L489: Additionally, to support the significant increase in business, the Board
L490: approved a private placement of 500,000 shares at $1.50 per share, which was
L491: subsequently increased to 1,204,855 shares. The Board also approved the sale of
L492: up to 21% equity in the Company to a minority partner. NetCom Solutions
L493: International subsequently purchased approximately 8% or 700,000 shares of the
L494: Company at $1.50 per share. As of March 2000, $930,000 of debt was converted to
L495: equity, $1.8 million was received by the private placement and $1.05 million in
L496: the form of cash and a short-term note was received from the sale of a minority
L497: interests.
L498:          The Company's principal capital requirements are increased working
L499: capital needed to support its growth and reduce outstanding accounts payable.
L500: The Company currently is funding its working capital requirements with cash
L501: generated by operations and a receivables factoring facility with a financial
L502: institution. As of June 1, 2001 the Company had $0.8 million in unrestricted
L503: cash and working capital of $0.3 million. During the quarter the Company used
L504: its credit line as well as extending payables with vendors to provide the
L505: working capital required. As a result of extending payables, the Company has
L506: moved to a cash basis with several major vendors which will constrain revenue
L507: recognition until additional working capital is in place. The cash balances
L508: going forward will be reduced by the need to immediately fund the acquisition of
L509: material from vendors until outstanding payables can be reduced as a result of
L510: obtaining additional working capital. The Company is seeking additional
L511: financing to reduce outstanding aged accounts payable and to provide the working
L512: capital to fund the increase in sales projected for 2001. In addition, the
L513: Company has contracted with F&H Financial to renegotiate amounts owed to vendors
L514: and expects working capital requirements to be reduced as a result.
